I-9 EMPLOYMENT ELIGIBILITY VERIFICATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the federal Form I-9 employment eligibility verification process that the Immigration Reform and Control Act (IRCA) requires an employer to complete for a new hire, in connection with Acme, Inc.'s hiring of Jordan Lee with a start date of October 1, 2026. It summarizes selected requirements of 8 U.S.C. § 1324a and its implementing federal regulations. It is not the Form I-9 itself, does not complete, replace, or substitute for that form, and does not state, verify, or determine Jordan Lee's actual identity, employment authorization, or immigration status.

FEDERAL PROHIBITION ON KNOWINGLY HIRING OR CONTINUING TO EMPLOY AN UNAUTHORIZED ALIEN
Federal law makes it unlawful for a person or entity to hire an alien for employment in the United States knowing the alien is an unauthorized alien, and separately makes it unlawful, once an alien has been hired, to continue employing that alien knowing the alien is or has become unauthorized to work. Acme, Inc.'s hiring process, including the hiring of Jordan Lee, operates within this federal framework.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It is unlawful for a person or other entity— (A) to hire, or to recruit or refer for a fee, for employment in the United States an alien knowing the alien is an unauthorized alien (as defined in subsection (h)(3)) with respect to such employment"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(a)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Immigration Reform and Control Act, hiring prohibition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  "It is unlawful for a person or other entity, after hiring an alien for employment in accordance with paragraph (1), to continue to employ the alien in the United States knowing the alien is (or has become) an unauthorized alien with respect to such employment."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Immigration Reform and Control Act, continuing-employment prohibition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the federal prohibition on knowingly hiring or continuing to employ an unauthorized alien — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual work authorization status. The statute does not state this prohibition as a single unified rule covering both hiring and continued employment in one sentence or subsection, as is sometimes assumed; it is split across two separate paragraphs of the same section — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(a)(1)(A) (the hiring prohibition) and 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(a)(2) (the separate continuing-employment prohibition, which applies only once an employer already knows, after the fact, that a previously hired alien is or has become unauthorized). Both citations below are to different subsections of this same statutory section (§ 1324a); this clause draws no conclusion from that structure other than that they are two distinct prohibitions. Separately, § 1324a(a)(3) provides an affirmative defense to the hiring prohibition — not quoted or relied on here — for a person or entity that establishes good-faith compliance with the verification requirements of subsection (b).

THE FEDERAL EMPLOYMENT VERIFICATION REQUIREMENT (FORM I-9 ATTESTATION)
Federal law requires an employer to attest, under penalty of perjury on a federally designated form, that it has verified a new hire is not an unauthorized alien by examining specified documents establishing identity and employment authorization. Acme, Inc. completes this attestation for Jordan Lee using Form I-9.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The person or entity must attest, under penalty of perjury and on a form designated or established by the Attorney General by regulation, that it has verified that the individual is not an unauthorized alien by examining"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, employment verification system, attestation requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  "Documents establishing both employment authorization and identity"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, employment verification system, documents establishing both identity and authorization (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  "Documents evidencing employment authorization"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, employment verification system, documents evidencing employment authorization only (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  "Documents establishing identity of individual"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1)(D) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, employment verification system, documents establishing identity only (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the federal Form I-9 attestation and document-examination requirement — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual identity or work authorization status. All four citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory paragraph, 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1); none is cited more than once, and this clause draws no conclusion from the fact that they share a common paragraph other than that they are components of one attestation-and-documentation scheme. Separately: the statute itself organizes acceptable documents into three categories — documents establishing both identity and employment authorization (subparagraph (B)), documents evidencing employment authorization only (subparagraph (C)), and documents establishing identity only (subparagraph (D)) — so this three-way structure is genuinely in the statutory text, not only in agency guidance. The specific labels "List A," "List B," and "List C" that appear on the Form I-9 and in USCIS's Handbook for Employers (Form M-274), however, are not the statute's own subparagraph labels — the statute uses lettered subparagraphs, not numbered "Lists." The implementing regulation examined for this clause, 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2, restates the same three-way document structure at § 274a.2(b)(1)(v) and separately uses the term "List B" once, in a specific provision about how a minor's Form I-9 is completed — so the List A/B/C terminology has at least partial regulatory and form-instruction pedigree, but this clause did not find "List A," "List B," and "List C" used as formal headings within the regulatory text itself, only within that one incidental reference.

TIMING OF EMPLOYMENT VERIFICATION
Federal regulations set a deadline, measured from the date of hire, for completing the employment-verification examination and Form I-9 documentation, with a different, same-day deadline for a hire expected to last less than three business days.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "an employer, his or her agent, or anyone acting directly or indirectly in the interest thereof, must within three business days of the hire"
  — 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2(b)(1)(ii) (Cornell LII text), Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, general verification deadline (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/8/274a.2)
  "An employer who hires an individual for employment for a duration of less than three business days must comply with paragraphs (b)(1)(ii)(A) and (b)(1)(ii)(B) of this section at the time of the hire."
  — 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2(b)(1)(iii) (Cornell LII text), Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, short-duration-hire exception (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/8/274a.2)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a federal verification-timing deadline — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual hire date or work authorization status. This clause corrects an assumption worth stating directly: the "three business days" deadline is not located in 8 U.S.C. § 1324a itself. This clause's drafter read the full statutory text of § 1324a(a) and (b) directly and found no specific number-of-days deadline for completing verification after hire anywhere in the statute; § 1324a(b)(3), in particular, addresses retention of the completed form, not the deadline for completing it. The three-business-day deadline exists only in the implementing regulation, 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2(b)(1)(ii)-(iii) — a distinction that matters because a regulation can be amended by the agency through notice-and-comment rulemaking without a change to the underlying statute. Both regulatory citations below are to the same C.F.R. section, § 274a.2(b)(1); this clause draws no conclusion from that overlap other than that they are the general rule and its short-hire exception.

FEDERAL CIVIL PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS
Federal law authorizes civil monetary penalties, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing, against an employer found to have knowingly hired or continued to employ an unauthorized alien, in one statutory dollar range, and authorizes a separate, lower statutory dollar range of civil penalties for paperwork or documentation violations of the Form I-9 verification requirement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "With respect to a violation of subsection (a)(1)(A) or (a)(2), the order under this subsection— (A) shall require the person or entity to cease and desist from such violations and to pay a civil penalty in an amount of— (i) not less than $250 and not more than $2,000 for each unauthorized alien with respect to whom a violation of either such subsection occurred, (ii) not less than $2,000 and not more than $5,000 for each such alien in the case of a person or entity previously subject to one order under this paragraph, or (iii) not less than $3,000 and not more than $10,000 for each such alien in the case of a person or entity previously subject to more than one order under this paragraph"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(e)(4)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, civil penalty for hiring and continuing-employment violations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  "With respect to a violation of subsection (a)(1)(B), the order under this subsection shall require the person or entity to pay a civil penalty in an amount of not less than $100 and not more than $1,000 for each individual with respect to whom such violation occurred."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(e)(5) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, civil penalty for paperwork violations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the existence and structure of two distinct federal civil-penalty ranges — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's or employer's actual liability or work authorization status. Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(e) — paragraph (4) (hiring and continuing-employment violations) and paragraph (5) (paperwork violations); this clause draws no conclusion from that shared subsection other than that they set different penalty ranges for different kinds of violations. The dollar figures quoted below are the amounts as codified in the U.S. Code text itself (originally set in 1986 and last amended in the statute in 1996). This clause did not independently verify the current, inflation-adjusted penalty amounts that DHS actually assesses today: those base statutory dollar amounts are subject to periodic upward adjustment under a separate law, the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act, implemented through DHS rulemaking (codified at 8 C.F.R. § 274a.10) rather than through amendment of § 1324a(e) itself, and this clause's drafter did not fetch or verify that separate inflation-adjustment regulation or its current dollar figures — an honest gap, disclosed rather than guessed at.

RETENTION OF FORM I-9 — NO FILING WITH A GOVERNMENT AGENCY
Federal law does not require an employer to submit or file a completed Form I-9 with any government agency at the time it is completed. Instead, federal law requires the employer to retain the completed form for a set period and make it available for inspection by specified federal officials if asked. Acme, Inc. retains Form I-9 for Jordan Lee accordingly.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "After completion of such form in accordance with paragraphs (1) and (2), the person or entity must retain a paper, microfiche, microfilm, or electronic version of the form and make it available for inspection by officers of the Service, the Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices, or the Department of Labor during a period beginning on the date of the hiring, recruiting, or referral of the individual and ending— (A) in the case of the recruiting or referral for a fee (without hiring) of an individual, three years after the date of the recruiting or referral, and (B) in the case of the hiring of an individual— (i) three years after the date of such hiring, or (ii) one year after the date the individual’s employment is terminated, whichever is later."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, retention of verification form (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the federal retain-and-make-available (rather than routinely file) structure for a completed Form I-9, and of the statutory retention period — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual work authorization status. The retention period under § 1324a(b)(3)(B), quoted below, is three years after the date of hiring, or one year after the date employment is terminated, whichever is later. The statute names the officials who may inspect the retained form as officers of "the Service," the Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices, and the Department of Labor. This clause's drafter did not independently re-verify, against a separate reorganization statute, exactly how "the Service" (the former Immigration and Naturalization Service) maps onto current DHS component agencies after the 2003 creation of DHS and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; the codified text of § 1324a itself still uses "the Service" and "the Attorney General" throughout, which this clause quotes as written rather than substituting current agency names.

SEPARATE FEDERAL PROHIBITION ON DISCRIMINATION IN THE VERIFICATION PROCESS
A separate federal statute prohibits an employer from discriminating against an individual, in hiring or in discharge, because of national origin or, for a protected individual, because of citizenship status, including when the employer is carrying out the employment-verification process described above. This prohibition exists independently of, and in addition to, the employment-verification requirement itself, and it does not apply to every employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It is an unfair immigration-related employment practice for a person or other entity to discriminate against any individual (other than an unauthorized alien, as defined in section 1324a(h)(3) of this title) with respect to the hiring, or recruitment or referral for a fee, of the individual for employment or the discharging of the individual from employment— (A) because of such individual’s national origin, or (B) in the case of a protected individual (as defined in paragraph (3)), because of such individual’s citizenship status."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, general prohibition on national-origin and citizenship-status discrimination (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "Paragraph (1) shall not apply to— (A) a person or other entity that employs three or fewer employees"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, small-employer exception (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that a distinct anti-discrimination protection is layered on top of the employment-verification requirement, not that the verification requirement itself is a discrimination statute — and not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, or about any specific individual's actual national origin, citizenship status, or work authorization status. Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a) — paragraph (1) (the general prohibition) and paragraph (2)(A) (an exception to it); this clause draws no conclusion from that shared subsection other than that the exception qualifies the general rule. The general prohibition, § 1324b(a)(1), does not apply to a person or entity that employs three or fewer employees, under § 1324b(a)(2)(A) — so, as quoted below, this protection has a small-employer carve-out that this clause's body does not itself state. § 1324b(a)(2) also contains two further exceptions not quoted here: one for national-origin discrimination already covered by Title VII of the Civil Rights Act as applied to a given employer, and one for citizenship-status discrimination that is otherwise required by law, regulation, executive order, or government contract.

ABOUT THIS DOCUMENT
This information sheet summarizes selected federal requirements under the Immigration Reform and Control Act. It is not the Form I-9, USCIS's Handbook for Employers (Form M-274), or any other official government form, and reading or retaining it does not by itself satisfy Acme, Inc.'s obligation to complete an actual Form I-9 for Jordan Lee. The current Form I-9 and its instructions are published by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
